title: Trunk Muscles
path: Major Muscle Groups of the Body

headings.title: Introduction to the Trunk Muscles
headings.content: The trunk muscles form the structural bridge between the upper and lower halves of the human body. Unlike the limbs, which specialize in reaching and locomotion, the primary duty of the trunk is protection and stabilization. These muscles encase the vital organs of the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities, providing a muscular wall that defends against physical trauma. They attach the vertebral column, ribs, and pelvis, creating a flexible yet remarkably strong column that allows bending, twisting, and upright standing without collapsing.

headings.title: Muscles of the Anterior and Lateral Abdominal Wall
headings.content:
The front and sides of the abdomen rely on four main muscle pairs arranged in overlapping layers. This layered design creates immense internal pressure to support lifting, defecation, and childbirth.

- **Rectus abdominis**: Runs vertically down the midline, separated by the linea alba, responsible for flexing the lumbar spine.
- **External oblique**: Superficial side muscles whose fibers run downward and medially, helping to rotate the trunk.
- **Internal oblique**: Lies beneath the external oblique with fibers running in the opposite direction for twisting support.
- **Transversus abdominis**: The deepest layer, wrapping horizontally around the abdomen like a natural corset to compress internal organs.

headings.title: Deep Muscles of the Back and Vertebral Column
headings.content: Supporting the spine from behind are the deep intrinsic back muscles, often grouped as the erector spinae and smaller segmental rotators. These muscles maintain an upright posture against the constant pull of gravity. When both sides contract together, they extend the back, lifting the chest upright from a bending position. When only one side contracts, they bend the spine laterally toward that same side. Keeping these deep posterior muscles conditioned is vital for preventing chronic low back strain during physical labor.

headings.title: The Diaphragm and Muscles of Respiration
headings.content: Breathing depends heavily on the trunk muscles acting inside the thoracic cavity. The **diaphragm** is a dome-shaped skeletal muscle separating the chest from the abdomen. During inhalation, it contracts and flattens downward, enlarging the chest cavity and drawing air into the lungs. Accessory breathing muscles, including the intercostal muscles located between the ribs, elevate the rib cage to expand breathing capacity further during exertion or respiratory distress.

headings.title: Functional Role in Posture and Core Stability
headings.content: Core stability is not just about having visible abdominal definitions; it is the coordinated activation of deep trunk muscles to create a stable cylinder of support. The transversus abdominis, diaphragm, pelvic floor, and deep back muscles fire simultaneously to increase intra-abdominal pressure before any limb movement occurs. This anticipatory stabilization protects the delicate spinal cord and prevents excessive shearing forces on the vertebrae during everyday lifting and walking.

headings.title: Clinical Relevance in Nursing and Patient Mobility
headings.content: Understanding trunk muscle mechanics is essential for safe patient care in clinical settings. Midwives and nurses regularly assess abdominal integrity after surgeries like Caesarean sections, where the rectus abdominis has been retracted or incised. Weakened or painful trunk muscles impair a patient's ability to cough effectively, increasing the risk of postoperative pulmonary complications. Furthermore, using proper body mechanics during patient transfers relies on engaging the nurse's own core stability to prevent debilitating occupational back injuries.
